guidance: Use cost per foot to compare bit runs on the same well plan: hold the rig rate and the trip time constant and change one bit at a time, because the ranking flips when the rig rate changes. Take the rate as the full operating cost of the rig per day, not only the drilling contractor rate, and take the footage and the hours from the same run and the same depth reference. The figure is a planning comparison of bit performance; it does not replace the well cost estimate or the drilling programme.
method: One bit run is priced from three inputs. The rig rate is entered per day and divided by 24 to give a cost per hour; total interval cost = bit cost + rig cost per hour x (time on bottom + round trip), and cost per foot = that total / footage. The published field form is CT = (B + CR (t + T)) / F, with B the bit cost, CR the rig cost per hour, t the drilling time, T the round trip and F the footage drilled. Because the page also reports the rate of penetration R = F / t, the same figure splits exactly into three parts: the rig while drilling CR / R, the round trip CR x T / F and the bit B / F, and the three rounded parts add back to the cost per foot; the cost per metre is the cost per foot divided by 0.3048. When a target cost per foot C is entered, the footage at which the same rate of penetration and the same trip time reach it solves C F = B + CR (F / R + T), so F = (B + CR T) / (C - CR / R). That solution only exists above the drilling-only cost CR / R, the floor the rig sets however far the bit goes, so a target at or below the floor is refused rather than reported as an enormous or negative footage. Inputs are limited to a bit cost of 0 to 10,000,000 dollars, a rig rate of 0 to 5,000,000 dollars per day, 0.01 to 5,000 hours on bottom, 0 to 5,000 round-trip hours, 0.1 to 200,000 ft of footage and a target of at most 100,000 dollars per foot; a blank target skips the footage estimate. Warnings appear for a zero rig rate, a round trip longer than the time on bottom, a rate of penetration above 200 ft/h, a bit below 5 percent of the interval cost and a target that needs more than four times the interval drilled. The model assumes one bit, one fixed rig rate, no re-runs, repairs or lost time, and an interval measured from one depth reference; it does not model day-rate escalation, mobilisation, consumables or trouble time, and it is a planning comparison of bit performance rather than a well cost estimate.

sources.title: DrillingFormulas, Drilling cost per foot: CT = (B + CR (t + T)) / F with CR the rig cost per hour; the worked example, a 27,000 dollar bit, 3,500 dollars per hour, 50 h drilling, a 12 h round trip and 5,000 ft, gives 48.8 dollars per foot.

DrillingManual, Drilling Cost Per Foot Formula & Limitations: cost per foot = (bit cost + rig cost x (drill time + trip time)) / interval, a comparison of bit performance that shifts with the rig operating cost and is only as good as its inputs.
